summary: This document addresses Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) applications that have no capability negotiation, such as those for IP prefixes or point-to-point pseudowires. It describes how to control whether state is advertised when a peer may not use it, to avoid wasted information.

plainLanguage.summary: LDP lets routers exchange label information over a session. Older applications just send their information without checking whether the other router wants it. This document adds a small message that says which of those applications the receiving router should stop sending.

questions: what is ldp state advertisement control
how to stop ldp advertising ip prefix labels
what is the ldp sac capability
subtitle: A way for an LDP router to tell its peer which older applications it does not want state for.

tldr.problem: Some LDP applications have no capability negotiation, so a router advertises state for them even when the session exists for another purpose, such as mLDP or ICCP.
tldr.mechanism: A new State Advertisement Control capability, TLV code 0x050D, carries one element per application, each with a bit that disables or enables the advertisement of that application's state.
tldr.outcome: Routers stop sending label bindings the peer cannot use. RFC 7473 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8223.

facts.label: Application types
facts.value: 1 IPv4 Prefix-LSPs, 2 IPv6 Prefix-LSPs, 3 FEC 128, 4 FEC 129

facts.label: TLV length
facts.value: 1 plus the number of SAC elements

facts.label: Fixed bits
facts.value: U set to 1, F set to 0, S set to 1

today: RFC 7473 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It was later updated by RFC 8223, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: Unwanted State
sections.content:
The LDP Capabilities specification, RFC 5561, lets two peer label switching routers negotiate capabilities for a feature. The point is to make sure no unnecessary state is exchanged unless the matching capability was negotiated first.

Newer LDP features and applications use that framework, including Typed Wildcard FEC in RFC 5918, the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol in RFC 7275, mLDP in RFC 6388, and L2VPN point-to-multipoint pseudowires in RFC 7338. The earlier LDP applications did not: a speaker would exchange application state with no negotiation at all.

The result is state that the peer has no use for. A router that opens a session with a provider edge router only to exchange ICCP state may still advertise label bindings for IP prefixes. In a dual-stack network, a router set up for both IPv4 and IPv6 may advertise both address families to a peer that only wants IPv4. The wasted traffic costs memory, processor time and network resources.

The usual workaround is to configure filtering policies on the router, which adds operational overhead and complexity. RFC 7473 replaces that with a signal in the protocol itself: an LDP speaker announces its disinterest in the state of specific applications, and the peer stops advertising it. The document also defines the mechanics for turning the advertisement on or off again during the life of a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers that run LDP can end up sending each other information the other one does not need. A session set up for one purpose, such as exchanging state between equipment in different chassis, also carries label information for ordinary IP routes. This document adds a way for a router to say which information it does not want.

sections.title: Non-negotiated LDP Applications
sections.content:
For applications that predate the capabilities framework, an LDP speaker advertises its application state to its peers as soon as the session is established, with no exchange of capabilities first. Two of these older applications are covered here:

  • Prefix-LSPs is the application that sets up label switched paths for IP routes by advertising label bindings for Prefix FECs, as defined in RFC 5036.
  • P2P-PWs is the application that signals FEC 128 and FEC 129 Layer 2 VPN point-to-point pseudowires using LDP, as defined in RFC 4447.

A state of such an application is called uninteresting state when it is of no interest to a router and need not be advertised to it. Uninteresting state need not appear in any LDP protocol message, and what counts as uninteresting depends on the application type.

For Prefix-LSPs, the uninteresting state covers anything to do with IP Prefix FECs, such as FEC label bindings and LDP Status. The document deliberately does not treat IP address bindings, the ones carried in the ADDRESS message, as uninteresting state, so they continue to be advertised. A router normally needs a peer's IP addresses to map an IP routing next hop to an LDP peer, and mLDP uses the peer's IP addresses to find its upstream router and to pick the outgoing interface. Disabling the advertisement of IP address bindings would break mLDP.

For P2P-PWs, the uninteresting state covers anything to do with FEC 128 and FEC 129, such as FEC label bindings, MAC address withdrawal and LDP PW Status.
sections.plainLanguage: The document covers two older LDP applications: setting up label-switched paths for IP routes, and signalling point-to-point Layer 2 VPN pseudowires. It also leaves one thing alone on purpose, the peer's IP addresses, because mLDP needs them to work.

sections.title: The State Advertisement Control Capability
sections.content:
The State Advertisement Control capability is a new capability parameter TLV, defined in line with Section 3 of RFC 5561. It carries one or more State Advertisement Control elements, and each element turns the advertisement of uninteresting state on or off for one application.

Three bits of the TLV are fixed. The U-bit MUST be set to 1, so that a receiver that does not know the TLV silently ignores it and carries on with the rest of the message. The F-bit MUST be set to 0. The S-bit MUST be set to 1 in an Initialization message and in a Capability message, because once a capability has been advertised it cannot be withdrawn.

The Length field of the TLV is computed as one plus the number of SAC elements, so a receiver can work out how many elements are present. Two elements give a Length of three octets.

Each SAC element is one octet. The D-bit controls the advertisement: 1 disables it and 0 enables it. When an element is sent in an Initialization message the D-bit MUST be set to 1. The App field names the legacy application type: 1 for IPv4 Prefix-LSPs, 2 for IPv6 Prefix-LSPs, 3 for FEC 128 P2P-PW and 4 for FEC 129 P2P-PW. Any other value in that field MUST be treated as an error. The Unused field must be zero on transmit and is ignored on receipt.

If a TLV carries more than one element, the elements MUST belong to distinct application types, and an application type MUST NOT appear more than once. A receiver that gets a malformed TLV SHOULD discard it and process the rest of the message. An element whose App field holds an undefined value MUST be ignored and discarded, and the rest of the TLV still processed.
sections.plainLanguage: The new capability is one small message with a type code of 0x050D. It holds a list of elements, one per application. Each element has a bit that says whether to send that application's information or not, and a field naming the application.

sections.title: Capability Procedures
sections.content:
The capability states the desire of one LSR to stop receiving unwanted state from its peer. It is unilateral and unidirectional: the receiver is not required to send anything similar back, which matches the procedures in Section 6 of RFC 5561.

Once the capability has been sent by one LSR and understood by its peer, the receiving LSR MUST NOT advertise any state related to the disabled applications towards the sender, until those applications are explicitly enabled again by a later capability update. If the disabling happens during the life of a session, the receiving LSR MUST also withdraw from the peer any state it had already advertised for the application that is now disabled.

A receiving LDP speaker that does not understand the SAC capability TLV MUST answer the sender with an "Unsupported TLV" notification, as described in RFC 5561. A receiver that understands the TLV but does not support one of the applications named in an element SHOULD skip that element silently and carry on with the rest of the TLV.

An LDP speaker sends the capability in an Initialization message when it has decided, through local configuration or a default policy, that it wants to disable Prefix-LSPs, P2P-PWs, or both, on that session. The elements then carry a D-bit of 1. If the peer supports the Dynamic Announcement capability, the speaker may also send the capability later in a Capability message, either to disable an application that was previously enabled or to enable one that was previously disabled. The receiver reacts to that message in the same way, and additionally withdraws or advertises the application state to match the update.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal is one-sided: the router that sends it does not expect an answer. Once the peer understands it, the peer stops sending the information that was switched off, and pulls back anything it sent earlier.

sections.title: Applicability Statement
sections.content:
These procedures can result in the disabling of label bindings for IP prefixes and for P2P pseudowires, so the document recommends they be used with care. The capability SHOULD be enabled on an LSR only through a configuration knob, which may be global or per LDP neighbour. An operator SHOULD enable it towards a neighbour only when it is known that the bindings exchanged with that neighbour are unnecessary and wasteful.

The document lists the typical sessions where this applies, together with the state that can be switched off: a session carrying only FEC 128 pseudowires can switch off IP prefix LSPs and FEC 129 pseudowires; a session carrying only pseudowires can switch off IP prefix LSPs; an IPv4-only or IPv6-only session on a dual-stack router can switch off the other address family and the pseudowires; and an mLDP-only or ICCP-only session can switch off IP prefix LSPs and the pseudowires.

Several points matter to an operator. Prefix-LSP state SHOULD be disabled on any targeted LDP session that exists only for ICCP or only for pseudowires. It MUST NOT be disabled on a targeted LDP session that exists for reasons related to remote loop-free alternate fast re-routing. In a remote network where that fast re-routing is enabled, it is RECOMMENDED not to disable Prefix-LSP state even on a session that is only for pseudowires or only for ICCP, because any remote neighbour could be picked as the node providing the alternate path. The capability SHOULD be used for Prefix-LSPs when the aim is to disable or enable all the prefix label bindings; to filter a subset, the existing label announcement filtering procedures should be used instead. Using filtering policies together with these procedures is allowed.

If a change is needed after the session is up, the peers need the LDP Dynamic Announcement capability. Where a peer does not support it, the alternative is to reset the LDP session so that the new capability is advertised during the next initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks operators to switch this on deliberately, per neighbour, and only where the extra information is genuinely wasted. It also warns against switching it off where a fast re-routing path depends on those labels.

sections.title: Operational Examples
sections.content:
Disabling everything on an ICCP session. Two provider edge routers hold an LDP session to exchange ICCP state for dual-homed devices. If both are provisioned not to exchange Prefix-LSP or P2P-PW state, each puts a SAC capability with four elements, one per application and each with the D-bit set to 1, into its Initialization message. On receipt, the other router disables the advertisement of IPv4 and IPv6 label bindings and of FEC 128 and FEC 129 signalling towards its peer once the session is established.

Disabling Prefix-LSPs on a pseudowire session. Two routers hold a targeted LDP session for FEC 128 and FEC 129 pseudowires. Since IP label bindings are rarely needed over such a session, both are provisioned to disable the Prefix-LSP application, and only pseudowire state is exchanged afterwards.

Disabling Prefix-LSPs during a session. Two routers that both support the Dynamic Announcement capability start out exchanging both kinds of state. When one is reconfigured to disable the Prefix-LSPs, it sends a SAC capability in a Capability message with elements for the IPv4 and IPv6 Prefix-LSPs and the D-bit set to 1. The peer disables those applications towards the sender and withdraws all the state it had advertised. To withdraw label bindings it MAY use a single Prefix FEC Typed Wildcard Label Withdraw message if the peer supports the Typed Wildcard FEC capability. The pseudowire signalling on the same session is unaffected.

Disabling Prefix-LSPs on an mLDP-only session. The peer stops advertising anything to do with IP Prefix FECs, but it still advertises IP address bindings, which mLDP needs to work.

Disabling one address family on a dual-stack router. One router runs Prefix-LSPs for both IPv4 and IPv6, while the other is interested only in IPv4. The second sends a SAC capability with an element for the IPv6 Prefix-LSPs and the D-bit set to 1 in the Initialization message, and the first stops advertising IPv6 label bindings towards it. If IPv6 is enabled later on the second router, it sends a Capability message to enable the application again.
sections.plainLanguage: The document walks through five situations: a session used only to talk between equipment in different chassis, a session used only for pseudowires, a session where the switch happens later, a session used only for multicast, and a dual-stack router that only wants one address family. In each case one router asks, and the other stops sending.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The proposal introduces no new security considerations beyond those that already apply to the base LDP specification in RFC 5036 and to MPLS and GMPLS in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security considerations of its own. The usual LDP and MPLS rules apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the code point 0x050D from the "TLV Type Name Space" in the "Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Parameters" registry to the new LDP capability TLV, described as the State Advertisement Control Capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the registry for one new code point, 0x050D, for the capability message.

fields.desc: Must be zero on transmit and is ignored on receipt.

messages.label: Initialization with SAC capability
messages.note: One element per unwanted application, each with the D-bit set to 1.

messages.label: State advertisement stops
messages.note: The peer no longer advertises label bindings for the disabled applications.

messages.label: Capability message with SAC capability
messages.note: Sent later if the peer supports Dynamic Announcement, to enable or disable an application.

messages.label: State withdrawn or advertised
messages.note: The peer withdraws state for a newly disabled application, or advertises it for a newly enabled one.
